title: Transformer Architecture

TensorFlow 2: Encoder Block

import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers

class TransformerEncoder(layers.Layer):
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_heads, dff):
        super().__init__()
        self.att = layers.MultiHeadAttention(num_heads, d_model)
        self.ffn = tf.keras.Sequential([
            layers.Dense(dff, activation='relu'),
            layers.Dense(d_model)
        ])
        self.norm1 = layers.LayerNormalization()
        self.norm2 = layers.LayerNormalization()

    def call(self, x):
        attn = self.att(x, x)
        x = self.norm1(x + attn)
        ffn = self.ffn(x)
        return self.norm2(x + ffn)

title: Transformer Architecture
text:
Query–Key–Value Framework
Each token is mapped to:

Query: \(\mathbf q\)
Key: \(\mathbf k\)
Value: \(\mathbf v\)

\[
\mathbf q = \mathbf W_Q^\top\mathbf x, \quad \mathbf k = \mathbf W_K^\top\mathbf x, \quad \mathbf v = \mathbf W_V^\top\mathbf x
\]

title: Transformer Architecture
text:
Attention Score
Similarity between tokens:
\[
\text{score}(\mathbf q, \mathbf k) = \mathbf q^\top \mathbf k
\]
Scaled:
\[
\frac{\mathbf q^\top \mathbf k}{\sqrt{d_k}}
\]

title: Transformer Architecture
text:
Attention Weights
\[
\alpha = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf q^\top \mathbf k}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)
\]
Interpretation:

importance of each word relative to another

title: Transformer Architecture
text:
Matrix Form

\(\mathbf Q = {[\mathbf q_1^\top\ \cdots \ \mathbf q_n^\top]}^\top = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf x_1^\top\mathbf W_Q\\ \vdots\\ \mathbf x_n^\top\mathbf W_Q\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\mathbf K = {[\mathbf k_1^\top\ \cdots \ \mathbf k_n^\top]}^\top = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf x_1^\top\mathbf W_K\\ \vdots\\ \mathbf x_n^\top\mathbf W_K\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\mathbf V = {[\mathbf v_1^\top\ \cdots \ \mathbf v_n^\top]}^\top = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf x_1^\top\mathbf W_V\\ \vdots\\ \mathbf x_n^\top\mathbf W_V\end{bmatrix}\)

title: Transformer Architecture
text:
Attention Output
\[
\text{Attention}(\mathbf Q, \mathbf K, \mathbf V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf Q^\top \mathbf K}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)\mathbf V
\]

Weighted sum of values
Context-aware representation

title: Regularisation for Neural Networks

What Is Regularisation?
Definition
Any technique that constrains learning to improve out-of-sample performance.
Three perspectives

Penalise complexity

Inject noise

Stop training early

title: Regularisation for Neural Networks
text:
Explicit Regularisation: L2 (Weight Decay)
\[
\mathscr{L}(\theta) = \mathscr{L}_{data}(\theta) + \lambda \sum_i w_i^2
\]
Effects

Penalises large weights
Encourages smooth functions
Improves conditioning

title: Regularisation for Neural Networks
text:
Geometric Interpretation of L2

Penalises distance from origin
Shrinks parameters continuously
Equivalent to Gaussian prior on weights

title: Regularisation for Neural Networks
text:
L1 Regularisation
\[
\mathscr{L}(\theta) = \mathscr{L}_{data}(\theta) + \lambda \sum_i |w_i|
\]
Key properties

Produces sparse solutions
Performs implicit feature selection
Less common in deep networks

title: Regularisation for Neural Networks
text:
Tensorflow Implementation

from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras import layers

model = keras.Sequential([
    layers.Dense(
        128,
        activation="relu",
        kernel_regularizer=keras.regularizers.l2(1e-3) ## L2 regularisation on weights
    ),
    layers.Dense(
        128,
        activation="relu",
        kernel_regularizer=keras.regularizers.l1(1e-3) ## L1 regularisation on weights
    ),
     layers.Dense(
        128,
        activation="relu",
        kernel_regularizer=keras.regularizers.l1_l2(1e-3) ## L1 and L2 regularisation on weights
    ),
    layers.Dense(1)
])

model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="mse"
)

Stochastic Regularisation

Forces robustness
Prevents co-adaptation

Examples:

Dropout
Noise injection

title: Regularisation for Neural Networks
text:
Dropout
Idea

Randomly drop neurons during training

\[
\widetilde{h} = h \cdot \text{Bernoulli}(p)
\]
Interpretation

Approximate ensemble learning
Strong regularisation effect







Warning


Not to be used on inference time!

title: Regularisation for Neural Networks
text:
Dropout: Practical Notes

Most effective in fully-connected layers
Typical rates: 0.1–0.5
Often unnecessary with BatchNorm

Tensorflow Implementation

model = keras.Sequential([
    layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dropout(0.3),

    layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dropout(0.3),

    layers.Dense(1)
])

model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="mse"
)

title: Regularisation for Neural Networks
text:
Normalisation Layers
Primary purpose:

Stabilise optimisation

Secondary effect:

Regularisation through noise or smoothing

title: Regularisation for Neural Networks
text:
Batch Normalization
For mini-batch \(B\):
\[
\widehat{x} = \frac{x - \mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_B^2 + \epsilon}}, \quad
y = \gamma \widehat{x} + \beta
\]

\(\mu_B\) and \(\sigma_B^2\) are batch statistics
\(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) are learnable parameters

title: Regularisation for Neural Networks
text:
Why BatchNorm Works

Reduces sensitivity to parameter scale
Allows higher learning rates
Improves gradient flow

title: Regularisation for Neural Networks
text:
BatchNorm as Regularisation

Uses batch statistics
Introduces stochastic noise
Noise depends on batch composition

Result

Reduced overfitting
Often replaces dropout

title: Regularisation for Neural Networks
text:
Limitations of BatchNorm

Depends on batch size
Poor with small batches
Not ideal for:

RNNs
Online learning
Transformers








Note


For inference, use moving averages of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) from training.

Layer Normalization

\[
\widehat{x} = \frac{x - \mu_{features}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{features}^2 + \epsilon}}

Why LayerNorm?

Regularisation effect

Why Not Train on all Data?
If we train and evaluate on the same data:

Model may memorize the data
Performance estimate becomes optimistic

This is called overfitting.

60% train / 20% validation / 20% test

Key principle:

title: Introduction to Machine Learning

The Core Idea
What Is k-Fold Cross-Validation?

Split data into k approximately equal folds
For each fold:

Train on k−1 folds
Test on the remaining fold

Aggregate performance metrics

\[
\text{CV score} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \text{Score}_i
\]

Genetic Algorithms for Hyperparameter Optimization
Idea
Treat each hyperparameter configuration as an individual in a population.
Example genome:
\[
\theta = (learning\ rate,\ batch\ size,\ dropout,\ layers)
\]
Each individual is evaluated by training the model and measuring validation performance.

Evolutionary Process

Initialize population with random hyperparameters
Evaluate fitness

\[

\]

Selection

Choose best-performing individuals

Crossover

Combine hyperparameters from two parents

Mutation

Randomly change some hyperparameters

Repeat for multiple generations



Advantages
✔ Works with non-differentiable objectives
✔ Naturally handles mixed hyperparameters
✔ Global search

Limitations
✖ Computationally expensive
✖ Slower convergence than Bayesian optimisation

title: Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
Bayesian Hyperparameter Optimization
Problem
Training a model with hyperparameters:
\[
\theta^* = \arg\min_{\theta} f(\theta)
\]
where

\(\theta\) - hyperparameters

\(f(\theta)\) - validation loss after training

Training the model is expensive, so we want to evaluate as few configurations as possible.

Key Idea
Instead of blind search, we build a probabilistic model of the objective function.
Typical surrogate models:

Gaussian Processes
Tree Parzen Estimators (Optuna)
Random Forest Surrogates



Intuition

Train model with hyperparameters ( _1 )
Observe validation loss
Update surrogate model
Choose next hyperparameters intelligently

title: Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
Bayesian Optimization Workflow
Algorithm

Sample a few hyperparameters randomly
Fit a surrogate model

\[
\hat{f}(\theta)
\]

Use an acquisition function to choose next hyperparameters

Common acquisition functions:

Expected Improvement (EI)
Probability of Improvement
Upper Confidence Bound


Exploration vs Exploitation
The acquisition function balances:



Exploration
Exploitation




Try uncertain regions
Try promising regions


Learn about space
Improve best result





Result
Bayesian optimisation finds good hyperparameters with far fewer trials than:

Grid search
Random search

title: Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
Visual Intuition of Bayesian Optimization

Surrogate Model
The expensive objective function (f()) is approximated by a probabilistic model:
\[
\hat{f}(\theta)
\]
Typically a Gaussian Process.
The model provides:

predicted mean
uncertainty estimate


Acquisition Function
The acquisition function selects the next hyperparameter configuration.
Example: Expected Improvement
\[
EI(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[\max(f_{best} - f(\theta),0)]
\]


Key Insight
The next evaluation is chosen where we expect maximum improvement, balancing:

promising regions

uncertain regions

Hyperband Algorithm for Hyperparameter Optimization
Motivation
Training models with many hyperparameter configurations is expensive.
Instead of fully training every configuration, Hyperband:

Quickly eliminates poor configurations and allocates resources to promising ones.


Core Idea
Hyperband uses successive halving.

Start with many hyperparameter configurations
Train each for a small number of epochs
Keep the best fraction
Increase training budget for survivors
Repeat until one configuration remains

from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
import optuna
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow import keras

X_train, y_train = make_regression(
    n_samples=100, n_features=5, noise=0.1
)
X_val, y_val = make_regression(
    n_samples=20, n_features=5, noise=0.1
)

def objective(trial):

    learning_rate = trial.suggest_float(
        "lr", 1e-5, 1e-2, log=True
    )

    n_units = trial.suggest_int("units", 32, 128)

    model = keras.Sequential([
        keras.layers.Dense(n_units, activation="relu"),
        keras.layers.Dense(1)
    ])

    optimizer = keras.optimizers.Adam(
        learning_rate=learning_rate
    )

    model.compile(
        optimizer=optimizer,
        loss="mse"
    )

    model.fit(X_train, y_train,
              validation_data=(X_val,y_val),
              epochs=10,
              verbose=0)

    loss = model.evaluate(X_val, y_val)

    return loss




Running Optuna

study = optuna.create_study(
    direction="minimize"
)

study.optimize(objective, n_trials=50)

print(study.best_params)

Mathematical View
Given data \((X, y)\):
At each node, choose split \(s\) that minimizes impurity:
\[
s^* = \mathop{\arg\min}_s \sum_{k \in \{L,R\}} \frac{n_k}{n} \, I(y_k)
\]
where \(I(\cdot)\) is an impurity measure.

\]

\[
\mathrm{Var}(y) = \frac{1}{n} \sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2

The optimal split minimizes weighted variance across child nodes.

Out-of-Bag (OOB) Error

Each tree in a
Random Forest
is trained on a bootstrap sample
~63.2% of observations are used
~36.8% are Out-of-Bag (OOB)

For each observation:

Collect predictions only from trees that did NOT see it

\[

\left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^n

\end{align*}
\]

Classification → Misclassification rate

Regression → MSE

\[
\text{OOB Error} =
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n
L(y_i, \widehat{y}_i^{OOB})
\]

title: Advanced Decision Trees
text:
Gradient Boosting: The Core Idea

Gradient Boosting builds an additive model
Models are trained sequentially
Each new tree:

Corrects the errors of the current model


General form: \[
F_M(x) = \sum_{m=1}^M \nu \cdot h_m(x)
\]
Where: - \(h_m(x)\): weak learner (tree) - \(\nu\): learning rate (shrinkage)
Key idea: > Improve the model step by step, not all at once

title: Advanced Decision Trees
text:
Gradient Boosting for Regression

Start with a constant model: \[
F_0(x) = \arg\min_c \sum_i (y_i - c)^2
\]
Compute residuals: \[
r_i = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i)
\]
Fit a tree to the residuals: \[
h_m(x) \approx r
\]
Update the model: \[
F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \nu h_m(x)
\]

Finance intuition:

Each tree explains what the previous model missed
Useful for returns, spreads, volatility

title: Advanced Decision Trees

Uses a classification loss (e.g. logistic loss)

At each step:

Compute the negative gradient of the loss
Fit a tree to this gradient
Update prediction scores

Interpretation:

Trees correct probability errors, not labels directly
Final output → probabilities via sigmoid

Vanishing Gradient Problem
Deep CNNs suffer from:

Gradient decay
Hard optimization
Solution: Residual Connections

title: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)
text:
Residual Connections
Introduced in:

He, K., Zhang, X., Ren, S., & Sun, J. (2015). Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition. arXiv:1512.03385.

Instead of learning:
\[HD(x)\]
Learn:
\[
F(x) = H(x) - x
\]
So:
\[
H(x) = F(x) + x
\]

title: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)
text:
Residual Block
Output:
\[y = F(x) + x\]
This is called a skip connection.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)

Easier optimization
Identity mapping available
Prevents degradation
Enables 100+ layer networks

title: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)
text:
Residual Block in TensorFlow

from tensorflow.keras import layers

def residual_block(x, filters):
    shortcut = x
    
    x = layers.Conv2D(filters, 3, padding='same', activation='relu')(x)
    x = layers.Conv2D(filters, 3, padding='same')(x)
    
    x = layers.Add()([x, shortcut])
    x = layers.Activation('relu')(x)
    
    return x

title: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)
text:
Full CNN with Residuals

inputs = tf.keras.Input(shape=(32,32,3))
x = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(32, 3, padding='same')(inputs)

x = residual_block(x, 32)
x = tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D()(x)

x = residual_block(x, 32)
x = tf.keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)

outputs = tf.keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax')(x)

model = tf.keras.Model(inputs, outputs)

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
section: Loss Functions: Why Do We Need Them?
text:
Loss Functions: Why Do We Need Them?
A neural network produces predictions:
\[
\widehat{\mathbf y} = \mathbf f_\boldsymbol\theta(\mathbf x)
\]
But how do we measure how wrong it is?
We define a loss function:
\[
\mathscr{L}(\mathbf y, \widehat{\mathbf y})
\]
Training objective:
\[
\min_{\boldsymbol \theta} \; \mathscr{L}(\mathbf y, \widehat{\mathbf y})
\]
The loss defines:

The optimization problem
The gradient signal
The statistical interpretation

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Regression Loss: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
Used for:

Regression
Continuous targets

Definition:
\[
\mathscr{L}_{MSE}
=
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (\mathbf y_i - \widehat{\mathbf y}_i)^\top (\mathbf y_i - \widehat{\mathbf y}_i)
\]
Properties:

Penalizes large errors heavily
Smooth and differentiable
Corresponds to Gaussian noise assumption

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
MSE: Gradient Intuition
For a single example:
\[
\mathscr{L} = \frac{1}{2}(y - \widehat{y})^2
\]
Derivative:
\[
\frac{\partial \mathscr{L}}{\partial \widehat{y}}
=
\widehat{y} - y
\]
Interpretation:

If prediction too large → positive gradient
If prediction too small → negative gradient

This becomes the error signal in backpropagation

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Binary Classification: Binary Cross-Entropy
Used for:

Spam detection
Credit default
Medical diagnosis

Output: probability
\[
\widehat{y} = \sigma(z)
\]
Loss:
\[
\mathscr{L}_{BCE}
=
- \left[
y \cdot \log (\widehat{y})
+
(1-y) \cdot \log(1-\widehat{y})
\right]
\]

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
section: Why Not Use MSE for Classification?
text:
Why Not Use MSE for Classification?
Problem:

Sigmoid saturates
Gradients become very small

Binary cross-entropy:

Strong gradients when wrong
Better probabilistic interpretation

With sigmoid + BCE: \[
\frac{\partial \mathscr{L}}{\partial z} = \widehat{y} - y
\]
Clean gradient → stable training

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Multiclass Classification: Cross-Entropy
Used for:

Digit recognition
Image classification
NLP tagging

Output: Softmax
\[
\widehat{y}_i =
\frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}
\]
Loss:
\[
\mathscr{L}_{CE}
=
- \sum_{i=1}^K y_i \log(\widehat{y}_i)
\]
Where:

\(y_i\) is one-hot encoded

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Training a Neural Network
Goal: \[
\min_{\boldsymbol \theta} \; \mathscr{L}(\mathbf y, \widehat{\mathbf y})
\]
Steps

Forward pass
Compute loss
Backpropagate gradients
Update parameters

Backpropagation: Intuition

Efficient application of the chain rule
Propagates error backward
Computes gradients for all weights

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
section: Backpropagation: What Problem Are We Solving?
text:
Backpropagation: What Problem Are We Solving?
We want to compute efficiently:
\[
\frac{\partial \mathscr{L}}{\partial w^{(l)}_{jk}} \quad \text{for all layers } l
\]
Naively:

Many parameters
Repeated computations








Key idea



Reuse intermediate derivatives
Apply the chain rule systematically

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Backpropagation: Chain Rule View
Forward pass: \[
\mathbf x \rightarrow \mathbf z^{(1)} \rightarrow \mathbf h^{(1)} \rightarrow \mathbf z^{(2)} \rightarrow \widehat{\mathbf y}
\]
Where: \[
\mathbf z^{(l)} = \mathbf W^{(l)} \mathbf h^{(l-1)} + \mathbf b^{(l)}
\] \[
\mathbf h^{(l)} = \sigma(\mathbf z^{(l)}) =[\sigma(z_1^{(l)}), \ldots, \sigma(z_{n_l}^{(l)})]^\top
\]
Backward pass: \[
\frac{\partial \mathscr{L}}{\partial \mathbf z^{(l)}} =
\frac{\partial \mathscr{L}}{\partial \mathbf z^{(l+1)}}
\frac{\partial \mathbf z^{(l+1)}}{\partial \mathbf z^{(l)}}
\]






Note


Errors flow backwards, data flows forwards

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Backpropagation: Error Terms
Define the error signal at layer \(l\):
\[
\boldsymbol \delta^{(l)} = \frac{\partial \mathscr{L}}{\partial \mathbf z^{(l)}}
\]

represents how much the loss would change if the pre-activation at layer \(l\) is changed
row vector of size \(1 \times n_l\)


Output layer: \[\begin{align}
\boldsymbol \delta^{(L + 1)} & =
\frac{\partial \mathscr{L}}{\partial \widehat{\mathbf y}} \text{diag} \left( \sigma'(\mathbf z^{(L + 1)}) \right) \\
& = \frac{\partial \mathscr{L}}{\partial \widehat{\mathbf y}} \odot \left( \sigma'\left(\mathbf z^{(L + 1)}\right) \right)^\top
\end{align}\]


Hidden layers: \[\begin{align*}
\boldsymbol \delta^{(l)}  & = \frac{\partial \mathscr{L}}{\partial \mathbf z^{(l)}} \\
& = \frac{\partial \mathscr{L}}{\partial \mathbf z^{(l + 1)}} \frac{\partial \mathbf z^{(l + 1)}}{\partial \mathbf h^{(l)}} \frac{\partial \mathbf h^{(l)}}{\partial \mathbf z^{(l)}} \\
& = \boldsymbol \delta^{(l+1)} \mathbf W^{(l+1)} \text{diag}\left(\sigma'\left(\mathbf z^{(l)}\right)\right) \\
& = \left( \boldsymbol \delta^{(l+1)} \mathbf W^{(l+1)} \right) \odot \left( \sigma'\left(\mathbf z^{(l)}\right) \right)^\top
\end{align*}\]

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Weight Gradients at Each Layer
\[
\frac{\partial \mathscr L}{\partial w^{(l)}_{jk}} = \frac{\partial \mathscr L}{\partial \mathbf z^{(l)}} \frac{\partial \mathbf z^{(l)}}{\partial w^{(l)}_{jk}} = \boldsymbol \delta^{(l)} \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \vdots \\ \underbrace{h^{(l-1)}_k}_{k^{\text{th}}\text{ position}} \\ \vdots \\ 0\end{bmatrix} =\delta^{(l)}_j h^{(l-1)}_k
\]

\[
\frac{\partial \mathscr L}{\partial \mathbf W^{(l)}} = \left(\boldsymbol \delta^{(l)}\right)^\top \left(\mathbf h^{(l-1)}\right)^\top
\]

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Bias Gradients at Each Layer
\[
\frac{\partial \mathscr L}{\partial b^{(l)}_j} = \frac{\partial \mathscr L}{\partial \mathbf z^{(l)}} \frac{\partial \mathbf z^{(l)}}{\partial b^{(l)}_j} = \delta^{(l)}_j
\]

\[
\frac{\partial \mathscr L}{\partial \mathbf b^{(l)}} = \left(\boldsymbol \delta^{(l)}\right)^\top
\]

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Toy Example: One Hidden Neuron
Model:

Input: \(x = 1\)
Hidden: \(h = \sigma(w_1 x)\)
Output: \(\widehat{y} = w_2 h\)
Loss: \(\mathscr{L} = \frac{1}{2}(y - \widehat{y})^2\)

Forward: \[
h = \sigma(w_1)
\]
\[
\widehat{y} = w_2 h
\]
Backward:
\[
\frac{\partial \mathscr{L}}{\partial w_2}
= (\widehat{y} - y) h
\]
\[
\frac{\partial \mathscr{L}}{\partial w_1}
= (\widehat{y} - y) w_2 \sigma'(w_1)
\]






Note


Error at output propagates backward to earlier weights

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Gradient Descent
Goal:
\[
\min_{\boldsymbol \theta} \; \mathscr{L}(\boldsymbol \theta)
\]
Update rule:
\[
\boldsymbol \theta \leftarrow
\boldsymbol \theta - \eta \nabla_{\boldsymbol \theta} \mathscr{L}(\boldsymbol \theta)
\]
Where:

\(\eta\) = learning rate
\(\nabla_{\boldsymbol \theta} \mathscr{L}\) = gradient
\(\boldsymbol \theta\) = all weights and biases

Interpretation:

Move parameters in the direction of steepest decrease.

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Stochastic & Mini-Batch Gradient Descent
Full gradient (expensive):
\[
\nabla_{\boldsymbol \theta} \mathscr{L}
=
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\nabla_{\boldsymbol \theta} \mathscr{L}_i
\]
Mini-batch gradient:
\[
\nabla_{\boldsymbol \theta} \mathscr{L}_B
=
\frac{1}{|B|}
\sum_{i \in B}
\nabla_{\boldsymbol \theta} \mathscr{L}_i
\]
Weight update:
\[
\boldsymbol \theta \leftarrow
\boldsymbol \theta - \eta \nabla_{\boldsymbol \theta} \mathscr{L}_B
\]
Why batching works:

The mini-batch gradient is an unbiased estimator of the true gradient: \[
\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{\boldsymbol \theta} \mathscr{L}_B]
=
\nabla_{\boldsymbol \theta} \mathscr{L}
\]
Much cheaper computationally
Adds useful noise → helps escape shallow minima

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Batches and Epochs
Definitions:

Batch size = number of samples used per update
Iteration = one parameter update
Epoch = one full pass through the dataset

If:

Dataset size = \(N\)
Batch size = \(B\)

Then:

Iterations per epoch = \(\frac{N}{B}\)





Example


\(N\) = 10000
Batch size = 100 → 100 updates per epoch




Why multiple epochs?

One pass is rarely enough
We refine weights gradually
Convergence requires repeated updates

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Momentum: Accelerating Gradient Descent
Problem with vanilla SGD:

Oscillates in narrow valleys
Slow convergence
Sensitive to noisy gradients








Idea


Accumulate a velocity vector in the direction of consistent descent.




Velocity update:
\[
\mathbf v_t = \beta \mathbf v_{t-1} + \nabla_\theta \mathscr{L}_B
\]
Weight update:
\[
\boldsymbol \theta_t =
\boldsymbol \theta_{t-1} - \eta \mathbf v_t
\]
Where:

\(\beta \in [0,1)\) = momentum coefficient (e.g. 0.9)
\(\mathbf v_t\) = exponentially weighted moving average of gradients

Intuition:

Smooths noisy updates

Speeds up motion along shallow directions

Reduces zig-zag behaviour

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
RMSProp: Adaptive Learning Rates
Problem with SGD + Momentum:

Same learning rate for all parameters
Some directions require smaller steps
Exploding updates in steep dimensions

Idea:

Scale the learning rate using a running average of squared gradients.

Compute running average:
\[
\mathbf s_t = \rho \mathbf s_{t-1} + (1-\rho)(\nabla_{\boldsymbol \theta} \mathscr{L}_B)^2
\]
Update rule:
\[
\boldsymbol \theta_t =
\boldsymbol \theta_{t-1}
-
\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{\mathbf s_t} + \epsilon}
\nabla_{\boldsymbol \theta} \mathscr{L}_B
\]
Where:

\(\rho \approx 0.9\)
\(\epsilon \approx 10^{-8}\)

Intuition:

Large gradients → smaller effective step

Small gradients → larger effective step

Each parameter gets its own adaptive learning rate

title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks in Finance
text:
Adam: Momentum + RMSProp
Adam = Adaptive Moment Estimation
Combines:

Momentum (1st moment)
RMSProp (2nd moment)

Step 1: First moment (mean of gradients)
\[
\mathbf m_t = \beta_1 \mathbf m_{t-1} + (1-\boldsymbol\beta_1) \nabla_\theta \mathscr{L}_B
\]
Step 2: Second moment (mean of squared gradients)
\[
\mathbf v_t = \beta_2 \mathbf v_{t-1} + (1-\beta_2) (\nabla_\theta \mathscr{L}_B)^2
\]
Step 3: Bias correction
\[
\widehat{\mathbf m}_t = \frac{\mathbf m_t}{1-\beta_1^t}
\quad
\widehat{\mathbf v}_t = \frac{\mathbf v_t}{1-\beta_2^t}
\]
Step 4: Parameter update
\[
\boldsymbol \theta_t =
\boldsymbol \theta_{t-1}
-
\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathbf v}_t} + \epsilon}
\widehat{\mathbf m}_t
\]
Typical defaults:

\(\beta_1 = 0.9\)
\(\beta_2 = 0.999\)
\(\epsilon = 10^{-8}\)

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
Why interpretability?
Modern ML models — random forests, gradient boosting, neural networks — are powerful but opaque. A single prediction may depend on hundreds of features through highly non-linear interactions.
We want to answer questions like:

Why did the model predict this for this instance?
Which features drive predictions overall?
How does the prediction change as a feature varies?
Can we trust the model on new data?

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
Two scopes of explanation


Local methods explain a single prediction (or a small neighbourhood).
Global methods describe the whole model: average effects, importances.
Model-agnostic = treats the model as a black box; works for any predictor.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
The running example
Throughout this deck we use the California housing dataset and a RandomForestRegressor trained on it.

Target: median house value (units of $100k).
8 numeric features: MedInc, HouseAge, AveRooms, AveBedrms, Population, AveOccup, Latitude, Longitude.
Held-out \(R^2 \approx 0.74\).

from sklearn.datasets import fetch_california_housing
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = fetch_california_housing(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=42)
model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, max_depth=12,
                              random_state=42, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
1. Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE)
Motivation
A Partial Dependence Plot (PDP) shows the average relationship between a feature and the prediction. But the average can hide:

Heterogeneous effects — opposite effects in different sub-populations that cancel out on average.
Interactions — the effect of feature \(X_j\) depends on the value of another feature.

Idea: show one line per instance instead of averaging.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
ICE — Theory
For each instance \(\mathbf{x}^{(i)} = (x_1^{(i)}, \dots, x_p^{(i)})\), we hold every feature fixed except \(X_j\). We then sweep \(X_j\) across a grid of values \(\{v_1, \dots, v_K\}\) and record the model’s predictions:
\[
\text{ICE}^{(i)}_j(v) = \widehat{f}\!\left(v,\, \mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{-j}\right)
\]
Plotting these curves gives one line per instance.
Centered ICE (c-ICE) anchors curves at a reference point \(a\) to compare shapes more easily:
\[
\text{c-ICE}^{(i)}_j(v) \;=\; \widehat{f}\!\left(v, \mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{-j}\right) \;-\; \widehat{f}\!\left(a, \mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{-j}\right)
\]
The PDP is just the average of the ICE curves.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
ICE — Example


Left: raw ICE curves diverge by intercept (different baselines).
Right: centered ICE makes shape differences visible — most curves rise similarly with MedInc, suggesting limited interaction here.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
ICE — Python
scikit-learn ships ICE/PDP in sklearn.inspection:
from sklearn.inspection import PartialDependenceDisplay
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(
    model, X_tr, features=["MedInc"],
    kind="both",            # "both" = ICE lines + average PDP
    subsample=80,           # subsample for clarity
    centered=True,          # produce c-ICE
    ax=ax,
)
plt.show()
Other packages: PiML, PDPbox (Python) and iml, pdp, ICEbox (R).
Pros & Cons

✔ Intuitive, reveals heterogeneity, model-agnostic.
✗ Only one feature at a time; can become a hairball; suffers from extrapolation when features are correlated (same issue as PDP).

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
2. LIME — Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations
Motivation
We want an answer to: “Why did the black-box model predict 0.83 for this instance?”
Idea (Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin, 2016): in a small neighbourhood, even a very complex function looks roughly linear. So fit a simple, interpretable model — a sparse linear model or a shallow tree — that is locally faithful to the black box.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
LIME — Example


The black-box model has a complex decision boundary.

We sample synthetic points around the instance of interest (yellow).

Each synthetic point is weighted by its proximity to the instance.

The weighted linear model (white line) is locally faithful to \(\widehat{f}\).

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
LIME — Python
import lime
import lime.lime_tabular

explainer = lime.lime_tabular.LimeTabularExplainer(
    training_data=X_tr.values,
    feature_names=X_tr.columns.tolist(),
    mode="regression",
    discretize_continuous=True,
)

exp = explainer.explain_instance(
    data_row=X_te.iloc[0].values,
    predict_fn=model.predict,
    num_features=6,
)

exp.show_in_notebook(show_table=True)   # or exp.as_pyplot_figure()
Packages: lime (tabular, text, image), eli5, interpret (Microsoft InterpretML).
Pros & Cons

✔ Works on tabular, text and images; intuitive coefficients.
✗ Instability: small changes in the neighbourhood (kernel width, sampling seed) can flip explanations; choice of kernel is itself an open problem.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
3. SHAP — SHapley Additive exPlanations
Motivation
LIME gives a local linear approximation, but its coefficients have no theoretical guarantees: change the kernel width and the explanation may change.
SHAP (Lundberg & Lee, 2017) borrows the Shapley value from cooperative game theory: a unique attribution scheme satisfying a small set of natural axioms.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
SHAP — Theory
Treat each feature as a “player” cooperating to produce the prediction \(\widehat{f}(\mathbf{x})\). The contribution of feature \(j\) is its Shapley value:
\[
\phi_j \;=\; \sum_{S \subseteq F \setminus \{j\}}
\frac{|S|!\,(|F| - |S| - 1)!}{|F|!}
\left[\, v(S \cup \{j\}) \;-\; v(S) \,\right]
\]
where \(v(S)\) is the model’s expected prediction when only the features in \(S\) are known.
Axioms uniquely characterising Shapley values:

Efficiency: \(\sum_j \phi_j \;=\; \widehat{f}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbb{E}[\widehat{f}(X)]\)
Symmetry: features with identical contributions get equal \(\phi\).
Dummy: a feature that never changes the output gets \(\phi = 0\).
Additivity: \(\phi\) of a sum of models = sum of the \(\phi\)’s.

Exact Shapley values cost \(\mathscr{O}(2^p)\) → SHAP provides efficient estimators:

KernelSHAP (model-agnostic, weighted linear regression).
TreeSHAP (exact, polynomial-time for tree ensembles).
DeepSHAP (approximations for neural networks).

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
SHAP — Example (single prediction)

A waterfall plot decomposes a single prediction \(\widehat{f}(\mathbf{x})\) from \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{f}(X)]\) (bottom) to the actual value (top), one feature at a time. Red pushes up, blue pushes down.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
SHAP — Example (global view)

The beeswarm plot stacks SHAP values across many instances. Each row is a feature, each dot an instance; colour encodes the original feature value.
→ MedInc dominates: high incomes (red) push predictions up; low incomes pull them down.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
SHAP — Python

import shap

# TreeSHAP — exact and fast for tree models
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model)
shap_values = explainer(X_te)             # an Explanation object

# Single prediction
shap.plots.waterfall(shap_values[0])

# Global summary
shap.plots.beeswarm(shap_values)
shap.plots.bar(shap_values)               # mean |SHAP| per feature (above)

# Model-agnostic alternative
kexp = shap.KernelExplainer(model.predict, shap.sample(X_tr, 100))
Packages: shap, also wrapped by interpret and alibi.
Pros & Cons

✔ Strong theoretical foundation; consistent local and global views.
✗ Exact computation expensive; for correlated features the “marginal” vs “conditional” expectations debate matters; TreeSHAP background-set choice affects results.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
4. Partial Dependence Plot (PDP)
Motivation
The simplest answer to “How does feature \(X_j\) affect predictions on average?”: fix every other feature at its observed values and average over them.
Friedman (2001) introduced PDPs as a tool to interpret gradient-boosted models.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
PDP — Theory
The partial dependence of the prediction on a subset of features \(X_S\) is:
\[
\widehat{f}_S(\mathbf{x}_S) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{X_C}\!\left[\, \widehat{f}(\mathbf{x}_S,\, X_C) \,\right]
\;\approx\; \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \widehat{f}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_S,\, \mathbf{x}_C^{(i)}\right)
\]
where \(C = \{1,\dots,p\}\setminus S\) are the “other” features.
The PDP is the mean of the ICE curves. It can be plotted in 1-D (one feature) or 2-D (an interaction). It assumes feature \(X_S\) is independent of \(X_C\) — when that fails, the average is taken over impossible combinations and the curve becomes misleading.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
PDP — Example


Left: 1-D PDP — predicted price rises steeply with MedInc, then flattens.
Right: 2-D PDP — for low occupancy, increasing MedInc increases price strongly; the joint effect is visible as the diagonal gradient.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
PDP — Python
from sklearn.inspection import PartialDependenceDisplay
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1-D and 2-D PDPs in a single call
PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(
    model, X_tr,
    features=["MedInc", "AveOccup", ("MedInc", "AveOccup")],
    grid_resolution=40,
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Packages: sklearn.inspection, PDPbox, PiML, interpret.
Pros & Cons

✔ Easy to compute, easy to read, supports 2-D interactions.
✗ Assumes feature independence — bias under correlation; hides heterogeneity (use ICE for that).

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
5. Accumulated Local Effects (ALE)
Motivation
PDPs break when features are correlated, because they evaluate the model at impossible feature combinations (e.g. a high Latitude with a low Longitude — outside California!).
ALE plots (Apley & Zhu, 2020) sidestep the problem: instead of averaging predictions, they average local differences of the prediction within small bins of the feature.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
ALE — Theory
Partition the range of \(X_j\) into \(K\) quantile bins \(\{(z_{k-1}, z_k]\}\). For each bin compute the average local effect:
\[
\widehat{\text{LE}}_k \;=\; \frac{1}{n_k} \sum_{i\,:\,x_j^{(i)} \in (z_{k-1}, z_k]}
\left[\, \widehat{f}(z_k,\, \mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{-j}) \,-\, \widehat{f}(z_{k-1},\, \mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{-j}) \,\right]
\]
The ALE is the cumulative sum of these local effects, centered to have mean 0:
\[
\widehat{\text{ALE}}_j(x_j) \;=\; \sum_{k\,:\,z_k\,\le\,x_j} \widehat{\text{LE}}_k \;-\; c
\]
The key insight: each \(\widehat{\text{LE}}_k\) only uses data inside the bin, so we never extrapolate outside the data manifold.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
ALE — Example

Left: Latitude and Longitude are strongly correlated (California’s shape). Right: PDP and ALE for Latitude disagree — ALE shows stronger location effects because it does not waste mass on impossible (Lat, Lon) combinations.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
ALE — Python
The most popular package is PyALE or alibi:
# Option A — alibi
from alibi.explainers import ALE, plot_ale
ale = ALE(model.predict, feature_names=X_tr.columns.tolist())
exp = ale.explain(X_tr.values)
plot_ale(exp, features=["Latitude"])

# Option B — PyALE
from PyALE import ale
ale_eff = ale(X=X_tr, model=model, feature=["Latitude"],
              grid_size=30, include_CI=True)
Packages: alibi, PyALE, interpret (partially); R has ALEPlot and iml.
Pros & Cons

✔ Unbiased under correlation; faster than PDP (no full-grid evaluation).
✗ Less intuitive (we plot cumulative local differences, not predictions); choice of bin count matters; only model-agnostic to first/second order.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
6. Permutation Feature Importance
Motivation
A direct, model-agnostic measure of how much the model depends on a feature:

If we destroy the information in feature \(X_j\) by randomly shuffling its values, how much worse does the model get?

Introduced by Breiman (2001) for random forests and generalised by Fisher, Rudin & Dominici (2019) for any model.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
Permutation Importance — Theory

Algorithm:

Compute the baseline error on a held-out set: \(e_{\text{orig}} = L(y, \widehat{f}(X))\).
For each feature \(j = 1, \dots, p\):

Permute column \(j\) of \(X\) (breaking the link with \(y\)).
Recompute the error \(e_{\text{perm}}^{(j)} = L(y, \widehat{f}(X^{\text{perm}_j}))\).

Importance: \(\text{PFI}_j \;=\; e_{\text{perm}}^{(j)} - e_{\text{orig}}\) (or the ratio).

Repeat the shuffle several times and average to reduce variance.
Watch out: when features are correlated, permuting one creates unrealistic instances; importance can be inflated or split across correlated features.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
Permutation Importance — Example

MedInc is by far the most important feature: shuffling it costs ~ 0.9 in \(R^2\). AveOccup, Latitude and Longitude follow.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning
text:
Permutation Importance — Python
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
import pandas as pd

result = permutation_importance(
    model, X_te, y_te,
    n_repeats=20,
    scoring="r2",
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1,
)

importances = pd.Series(result.importances_mean,
                        index=X_te.columns).sort_values(ascending=False)
print(importances)
Packages: sklearn.inspection, eli5.show_weights, rfpimp (handles correlated features via “drop-column” importance).
Pros & Cons

✔ Compresses everything into one number per feature; model-agnostic.
✗ Depends on the loss and dataset (train vs test); biased by feature correlation; says nothing about the direction or shape of the effect.

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Log-Return
\[r_t(n) = \ln\left(\frac{C_t}{C_{t-n}}\right)\]
Motivation: Log-returns are symmetric, additive over time, and approximately normally distributed — the standard unit of measurement in quantitative finance.
Interpretation:

\(r > 0\) appreciation
\(r < 0\) depreciation.

Typical periods: \(n = 1, 5, 10, 20\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Realised Volatility
\[\sigma_n = \text{std}\!\left(\{r_{t-n+1}, \ldots, r_t\}\right)\]
Motivation: Rolling standard deviation of log-returns is the most direct empirical measure of price uncertainty. Captures regime changes between calm and turbulent markets.
Interpretation:

Low = calm/trending regime
rising = growing uncertainty
high = crisis or event-driven.

Typical periods: \(n = 5, 10, 20, 60\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Overnight Gap
\[\text{Gap}_t = \ln\!\left(\frac{O_t}{C_{t-1}}\right)\]
Motivation: News, earnings, and macro events accumulate after hours. The overnight gap captures the information shock that arrives between sessions and cannot be hedged intraday.
Interpretation:

\(> 0\) gap up (positive overnight news)
\(< 0\) gap down (negative news).

Persistent gaps in one direction signal trend continuation.

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Intraday Range
\[\text{Range}_t = \frac{H_t - L_t}{C_t}\]
Motivation: The High-Low spread normalised by Close measures intraday uncertainty independent of price level. Reacts to news within the same session, before close-to-close volatility can update.
Interpretation:

Low = quiet session
spike = news or event
persistently high = volatile regime.

No lookback parameter — uses the current bar only.

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
ATR — Average True Range
\[\text{TR}_t = \max(H_t - L_t,\ |H_t - C_{t-1}|,\ |L_t - C_{t-1}|)\] \[\text{ATR}(n) = \text{mean}(\text{TR},\, n) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \text{TR}_{t-n+i}\]
Motivation: Extends the simple H-L range to account for overnight gaps. The standard input for volatility-scaled position sizing and stop-loss placement.
Interpretation:

Rising = volatility expanding
falling = contracting.

Common stop rule: \(k \times \text{ATR}\) with \(k = 1.5\)–\(3\). Typical periods: \(n = 7, 14, 21\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Garman-Klass / Parkinson Estimator
\[\hat{\sigma}^2_{GK} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\ln^2\!\frac{H_i}{L_i} - (2\ln 2 - 1)\ln^2\!\frac{C_i}{O_i}\right]\]
Motivation: Close-to-close volatility discards intraday information. The Garman-Klass estimator uses the full OHLC bar, achieving 5–8× lower variance than the standard estimator for the same window.
Interpretation: Same scale as realised volatility. Preferred for short windows or when intraday data is unavailable. Typical periods: \(n = 5, 10, 20\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
SMA Crossover
\[\text{SMA}(n)_t = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} C_{t-i}, \qquad \text{Signal} = \frac{\text{SMA}(s)}{\text{SMA}(l)} - 1\]
Motivation: Simple moving averages smooth price noise and reveal trend direction. The ratio of short to long SMA quantifies how much the recent trend deviates from the longer-term baseline.
Interpretation:

\(> 0\) bullish (short above long)
\(< 0\) bearish; zero-crossing signals a trend change.

Typical pairs: \(s/l = 5/20\), \(10/50\), \(50/200\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
EMA Crossover (Exponential Moving Average)
\[\text{EMA}(n)_t = \alpha\, C_t + (1-\alpha)\,\text{EMA}(n)_{t-1}, \quad \alpha = \tfrac{2}{n+1}\] \[\text{Signal} = \frac{\text{EMA}(s)}{\text{EMA}(l)} - 1\]
Motivation: EMA assigns exponentially decaying weights to past prices, making it more responsive to recent moves than SMA. Reduces lag at the cost of slightly more noise sensitivity.
Interpretation: Same directional logic as SMA crossover but reacts faster; more susceptible to whipsaws in ranging markets.
Typical pairs: \(s/l = 12/26\), \(9/21\), \(5/20\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
MACD Signal Line (Moving Average Convergence/Divergence)
\[\text{MACD}_t = \text{EMA}(s)_t - \text{EMA}(l)_t\] \[\text{Normalised} = \frac{\text{MACD}_t}{C_t}\]
Motivation: Measures the convergence and divergence of two EMAs, revealing momentum shifts before price crossovers occur. Normalising by price makes it comparable across instruments.
Interpretation:

Positive and rising = bullish momentum building
MACD crosses signal line = entry/exit
histogram shrinking = momentum weakening.

Standard parameters: \(s=12\), \(l=26\), signal \(=9\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
ADX — Average Directional Index
\[\text{ADX}(n) = \text{EMA}\!\left(\frac{|{+DI} - ({-DI})|}{+DI + (-DI)},\, n\right) \times 100\]
Motivation: Most trend indicators show direction but not strength. ADX is direction-agnostic — it measures how strongly price is trending regardless of whether up or down.
Interpretation: \(< 20\) ranging; \(20\)–\(25\) developing trend; \(> 25\) strong trend; \(> 40\) very strong. Pair with any crossover for direction. Typical periods: \(n = 7, 14, 21\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Parabolic SAR
\[\text{SAR}_{t+1} = \text{SAR}_t + \alpha\,(\text{EP} - \text{SAR}_t)\] \[ \alpha_0 = 0.02,\ \alpha_{\max} = 0.20\]
Motivation: A dynamic trailing stop that accelerates as a trend extends. Provides both a binary regime signal (above/below price) and a quantitative distance measure.
Interpretation:

Price \(>\) SAR = uptrend
Price \(<\) SAR = downtrend; SAR flip = reversal signal.

As a model feature encode as binary or \((C - \text{SAR})/C\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Rate of Change (ROC)
\[\text{ROC}(n)_t = \ln\!\left(\frac{C_t}{C_{t-n}}\right)\]
Motivation: The simplest and most direct momentum measure — the log-return over a fixed lookback. Captures the cross-sectional momentum anomaly documented extensively in academic literature.
Interpretation: \(> 0\) positive momentum; \(< 0\) negative; magnitude = strength. Use one feature per lookback. Typical periods: \(n = 5, 10, 20, 60\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
RSI — Relative Strength Index
\[\text{RS} = \frac{\overline{\text{Gain}(n)}}{\overline{\text{Loss}(n)}}\ , \, \text{RSI}(n) = 100 - \frac{100}{1 + \text{RS}}\]
Motivation: Compares average up-moves to average down-moves over a window, producing a bounded oscillator \([0, 100]\). Normalises momentum by recent range, making it comparable across volatility environments.
Interpretation:

\(> 70\) overbought
\(50\) neutral
\(< 30\) oversold.

The 50 line acts as a trend filter in many systems. Typical periods: \(n = 7, 14, 21\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Stochastic Oscillator %K / %D
\[\text{\%K}(n) = \frac{C_t - L_n}{H_n - L_n} \times 100, \, \text{\%D}(m) = \text{SMA}(\text{\%K},\, m)\]
Motivation: Measures where the current close sits within the recent High-Low range. In an uptrend, closes tend toward the top of the range; in a downtrend, toward the bottom.
Interpretation:

\(> 80\) overbought
\(< 20\) oversold
\(\text{\%K}\) crosses \(\text{\%D}\) = entry signal.

Typical params: \(n = 14\), \(m = 3\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Williams %R
\[\text{\%R}(n) = -100 \times \frac{H_n - C_t}{H_n - L_n}\]
Motivation: The inverse of Stochastic %K, emphasising proximity to the recent high. Mathematically \(\text{\%R} = \text{\%K} - 100\). Highly correlated with Stochastic — in a lean feature set use one or decorrelate.
Interpretation:

\(0\) to \(-20\) overbought
\(-50\) neutral
\(-80\) to \(-100\) oversold.

Typical periods: \(n = 7, 14, 21\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
CCI — Commodity Channel Index
\[\text{TP}_t = \frac{H_t + L_t + C_t}{3}, \qquad \text{CCI}(n) = \frac{\text{TP}_t - \text{SMA}(\text{TP},n)}{0.015 \times \text{MAD}(\text{TP},n)}\]
Motivation: Measures how many mean absolute deviations the typical price is from its moving average. The 0.015 constant places ~70–80% of values in \([-100, +100]\) under normal conditions, combining momentum and mean-reversion signals.
Interpretation:

\(> +100\) strong uptrend/overbought
\(0\) neutral
\(< -100\) strong downtrend/oversold.

Typical periods: \(n = 10, 14, 20\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Volume Log-Change
\[\Delta V_t = \ln\!\left(\frac{V_t}{V_{t-1}}\right)\]
Motivation: Volume is a proxy for market participation and conviction. Log-change normalises for wide variation in absolute volume across instruments and time.
Interpretation:

Price up + vol spike = confirmed breakout
price up + low vol = weak move
price down + vol spike = panic selling.

Divergence between price and volume often precedes reversals.

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Volume Ratio
\[\text{VR}(n)_t = \frac{V_t}{\text{SMA}(V,\, n)_t}\]
Motivation: Raw volume is not comparable across instruments or through time. Normalising by rolling average produces a dimensionless activity score indicating whether current participation is above or below its historical norm.
Interpretation:

\(\approx 1\) normal
\(> 1.5\) above-average interest
\(> 2\) unusual/event-driven
\(< 0.5\) unusually quiet.

Typical periods: \(n = 10, 20, 50\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
OBV / Rolling Mean
\[\text{OBV}_t = \text{OBV}_{t-1} + \begin{cases} +V_t & C_t > C_{t-1} \\ -V_t & C_t < C_{t-1} \\ 0 & C_t = C_{t-1} \end{cases}\] \[\text{Feature} = \frac{\text{OBV}_t}{\text{SMA}(\text{OBV},\, n)_t}\]
Motivation: Cumulative volume signed by price direction. Rising OBV with flat price indicates accumulation; falling OBV with rising price signals distribution and potential reversal.
Interpretation:

OBV rising + price flat = accumulation
OBV falling + price flat = distribution
OBV confirms trend = high conviction move.

Typical normalisation periods: \(n = 10, 20\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
VWAP
\[\text{VWAP}(n)_t = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=t-n+1}^{t} C_i\, V_i}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=t-n+1}^{t} V_i}\]
Motivation: The volume-weighted average price — the fair value benchmark used by institutional traders. Represents the average price paid per share: both a mean-reversion anchor and an execution quality benchmark.
Interpretation:

Price \(>\) VWAP = bullish intraday bias
price \(<\) VWAP = bearish
crossing VWAP = mean-reversion signal.

Best suited for intraday data; use rolling VWAP for daily bars.

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
CMF — Chaikin Money Flow
\[\text{MFV}_t = V_t \cdot \frac{(C_t - L_t) - (H_t - C_t)}{H_t - L_t}\] \[\text{CMF}(n) = \frac{\sum \text{MFV}}{\sum V}\]
Motivation: Weights volume by where the close falls within the bar’s range. A close near the high implies buying pressure; near the low implies selling pressure. Summing over a window reveals sustained accumulation or distribution.
Interpretation:

\(> +0.25\) strong buying
\(0\) to \(+0.25\) moderate accumulation
\(-0.25\) to \(0\) distribution
\(< -0.25\) strong selling.

Typical periods: \(n = 10, 20, 21\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Bollinger Band Position
\[\text{BB}\%(n) = \frac{C_t - \text{SMA}(n)_t}{2\,\sigma_n}\]
Motivation: Defines a dynamic envelope around price based on rolling standard deviation. The position within the bands quantifies how stretched price is relative to recent volatility — the core of mean-reversion strategies.
Interpretation:

\(+1\) at upper band (overbought)
\(0\) at SMA (neutral)
\(-1\) at lower band (oversold).

Band width itself is a volatility regime indicator. Typical periods: \(n = 10, 20, 50\).

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Distance from 52-Week High / Low
\[d_{\text{high}}(n) = \frac{C_t - \max(C,\, n)}{C_t}, \qquad d_{\text{low}}(n) = \frac{C_t - \min(C,\, n)}{C_t}\]
Motivation: 52-week highs and lows are psychologically and structurally significant price levels. Breakouts above the 52-week high have strong documented momentum effects; proximity to the low captures distress or value.
Interpretation:

Near 52w high = momentum or resistance
breaking 52w high = strong breakout signal
near 52w low = distress or value opportunity.

Typical periods: \(n = 52, 26, 13\) weeks.

title: Technical Trading Indicators
text:
Z-Score of Price
\[Z(n)_t = \frac{C_t - \text{SMA}(n)_t}{\sigma_n}\]
Motivation: Places current price in a standardised statistical context — how many standard deviations from its recent mean. The cleanest, most model-friendly mean-reversion feature, especially useful for pairs trading and stat-arb strategies.
Interpretation:

\(> +2\) statistically overbought
\(\approx 0\) near mean
\(< -2\) statistically oversold.

Near-identical to BB% with the same \(n\) — one may be redundant. Typical periods: \(n = 20, 60, 120\).
